question: For each protein sequence in the input CSV, generate a redesigned sequence by replacing each amino acid with a randomly chosen member of its conservative functional group (aliphatic, aromatic, positive, negative, polar uncharged, sulfur-containing, polar amide, or proline). The redesigned sequence must be the same length as the original.

files.eval_guideline: The redesigned_sequence must be the same length as original_sequence with each position conservatively substituted within its functional group; column order may differ.
files.match_reasoning: The filenames are the same (redesigned_proteins.csv) and both are CSV files. This is the only candidate output, and it matches the redesign task.

parameters.question: Each residue is replaced by a RANDOMLY chosen member of its conservative functional group, so redesigned_sequence will legitimately differ from the reference letter-by-letter. Do not require string equality of redesigned_sequence. For each row verify: (1) original_sequence (and its ID) matches the reference; (2) redesigned_sequence has exactly the same length as original_sequence; (3) every position of redesigned_sequence is an amino acid from the same conservative group as the corresponding original residue, using groups: aliphatic (G,A,V,L,I), aromatic (F,Y,W), positive (K,R,H), negative (D,E), polar uncharged (S,T), sulfur-containing (C,M), polar amide (N,Q), proline (P). Column order may differ. Judge compliance with these rules, not identity of the random draws.

files.strategy_reasoning: The substitutions are drawn at random within each functional group, so the redesigned sequences cannot match the reference character-for-character and exact/approximate cell comparison would wrongly score 0; the guideline instead specifies rule-based criteria (equal length, within-group substitution) that require per-row semantic judgment, which 'summary' distribution statistics cannot perform.

comparison_details.explanation:
Structural alignment: Both files have shape (1, 3) with identical column names and order ['sequence_id', 'original_sequence', 'redesigned_sequence']. The single row aligns unambiguously via sequence_id = 'test_protein', and the 'original_sequence' values are byte-identical (60-residue hemoglobin-beta N-terminal fragment: MVHLTPEEKSAVTALWGKVNVDEVGGEALGRLLVVYPWTQRFFESFGDLSTPDAVMGNPK). So 2 of 3 columns match exactly.

The 'redesigned_sequence' column is the product of a randomized procedure, so exact string equality is neither expected nor a valid equivalence criterion. Per the evaluation guideline, the correct test is (a) equal length and (b) per-position conservative substitution within the residue's functional group.

Length check: reference redesigned = 60 residues; candidate redesigned = 60 residues; original = 60 residues. All equal.

Per-position group check of the candidate (MVHLT... -> CGHVS...), using groups aliphatic {G,A,V,L,I}, aromatic {F,W,Y}, positive {K,R,H}, negative {D,E}, polar uncharged {S,T}, sulfur {C,M}, amide {N,Q}, proline {P}: M->C (sulfur), V->G, H->H (positive), L->V, T->S (polar), P->P (proline preserved), E->D, E->D (negative), K->H (positive), S->S, A->I, V->L, T->S, A->G, L->G, W->F (aromatic), G->A, K->H, V->I, N->N (amide), V->I, D->D, E->E, V->A, G->L, G->I, E->E, A->G, L->A, G->L, R->R, L->V, L->A, V->A, V->V, Y->F, P->P, W->W, T->S, Q->Q, R->R, F->Y, F->W, E->D, S->T, F->Y, G->G, D->E, L->G, S->T, T->T, P->P, D->D, A->G, V->A, M->M (sulfur), G->G, N->N, P->P, K->R. All 60 positions are in-group; every proline is retained, no charge inversions, no aromatic/aliphatic crossovers.

I applied the same check to the reference redesigned sequence and it is likewise fully in-group (e.g., H->R, W->Y, N->Q, K->H, M->M), confirming both outputs are valid draws from the same specified distribution.

Assessment: no missing values, no extra/missing rows or columns, no identifier mismatches. The only difference is the specific random realization of the redesigned sequence, which is inherent to the task. Both satisfy the stated correctness criteria identically. Slight deduction from 1.0 only because the redesigned strings are not literally identical (candidate differs from reference at most positions) and the comparison therefore rests on specification compliance rather than value equality; the files are functionally equivalent.
